This paper presents a general model-free RL algorithm that leverages model-based representations to achieve the sample efficiency and performance of model-based methods, without the computational overhead. A recent surge of high-performing model-free RL algorithms with dynamics-based representations (Guo et al., 2020; 2022; Schwarzer et al., 2020; 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Fujimoto et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Scannell et al., 2024) has showcased the potential of this family of algorithms when tailored for a single benchmark. Recognizing the similarity between these modelbased and model-free approaches, our hypothesis is that the true benefit of model-based objectives is in the implicitly learned representation, rather than the model itself, and thus prompting the question: Can model-based representations alone enable sample-efficient general-purpose learning? Our proposed approach is based on learning features that approximately capture a linear relationship between state-action pairs and value. To do so, we draw heavily from modern dynamics-based representation learning methods (see Related Work) as well as the work of Parr et al. (2008), who show that both model-based and model-free objectives converge to the same solution in linear space. By mapping states and actions into a single, unified embedding, we eliminate any environmentspecific characteristics of the input space and allow for a standardized set of hyperparameters. We evaluate our method, MR.Q, on four widely used RL benchmarks and 118 environments, and achieve competitive performance against state-of-the-art domain-specific and general baselines without algorithmic or hyperparameter changes between environments or benchmarks.', 'section': 'INTRODUCTION', 'sec_num': '1'}, {'text': 'General-purpose RL. Although many traditional RL methods are general-purpose in principle, practical constraints often force assumptions about the task domain. For example, algorithms like Q-learning and SARSA (Watkins, 1989; Rummery & Niranjan, 1994) can be conceptually extended to continuous spaces, but are typically implemented using discrete lookup tables. In practice, early examples of general decision-making approaches can be found in on-policy methods with function approximation. For instance, both evolutionary algorithms (Rechenberg, 1978; Back, 1996; Rubinstein, 1997; Salimans et al., 2017) and policy gradient methods (Williams, 1992; Sutton et al., 1999; Schulman et al., 2015; 2017) offer update rules with convergence guarantees and independence to the input space. However, despite their generality, these methods are also hindered by poor sample efficiency and are prone to local minima, limiting their suitability for many practical applications. In contrast, the design of deep RL algorithms tends to favor more specialized approaches that align closely with a single benchmark—e.g., DQN Atari (Bellemare et al., 2013; Mnih et al., 2015), DDPG MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012; Lillicrap et al., 2015), or AlphaGo Go (Silver et al., 2016). Generalizing beyond these initial benchmarks can often require significant engineering, tuning, or algorithmic discovery (Luong et al., 2019; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Haydari & Yılmaz, 2020; Ibarz et al., 2021). In imitation learning, GATO achieved generalist behavior, but relied on large expert datasets (Reed et al., 2022). Recently, DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2023) demonstrated a strong capability over many benchmarks without re-tuning, but used costly large models and simulated rollouts. Our objective is to discover a lightweight model-free approach to general-purpose learning. Dynamics-based representation learning. Building representations from system dynamics is a long-standing approach for adaptation, partial observability, and feature selection (Dayan, 1993; Littman & Sutton, 2001; Parr et al., 2008). Numerous model-free methods have been developed to learn representations by predicting future latent states (Munk et al., 2016; Van Hoof et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Gelada et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; 2022; Schwarzer et al., 2020; 2023; Zintgraf et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021; 2022; Fujimoto et al., 2021; 2024; McInroe et al., 2021; Seo et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Ni et al., 2024; Scannell et al., 2024). Unsurprisingly, these model-free approaches closely relate to model-based counterparts which learn a latent dynamics model for planning or value estimation (Watter et al., 2015; Finn et al., 2016; Karl et al., 2017; Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; 2021; Ye et al., 2021; Hansen et al., 2022; 2024; Hafner et al., 2019; 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Our approach, MR.Q, is most closely related to the state-action representation learning in TD7 (Fujimoto et al., 2024). At a high level, MR.Q differs from TD7 by discarding the original input and including losses over the reward and termination. MR.Q also differs significantly in implementation, drawing inspiration from prior work to determine a set of design choices that performs well across benchmarks, including multi-step returns, unrolled dynamics, and categorical losses. Our motivation also relates to linear MDPs (Jin et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2020) and linear spectral representation (Ren et al., 2022; 2023; Zhang et al., 2022; Shribak et al., 2024). The latter aims to learn a low-rank decomposition of the transition dynamics of the MDP and recover a linear relationship between an embedding and the value function. Similarly, our work connects to two-stage linear RL, where a non-linear embedding is learned for linear RL (Levine et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2019). State abstraction. Drawing inspiration from the theory of model-based representation learning, MR.Q demonstrates that model-free deep RL is a promising avenue for building general-purpose algorithms that achieve high performance across environments, while being simpler and less expensive than model-based alternatives. Our work also reveals insights on which design choices matter when building general-purpose model-free deep RL algorithms and how common benchmarks respond to these design choices. Model-based and model-free RL. MR.Q integrates model-based objectives with a model-free backbone during training, effectively blurring the boundary between traditional model-based and model-free RL. While MR.Q could be extended to the model-based setting by incorporating planning or simulated trajectories with the state-action encoder, these components can add significant execution time and increase the overall complexity and tuning required by a method. Moreover, the performance of MR.Q in these common RL benchmarks demonstrates that these model-based components may be simply unnecessary—suggesting that the representation itself could be the most valuable aspect of model-based learning, even in methods that do use planning. This argument is echoed by DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2, which rely on short planning horizons and trajectory generation, while including both value functions and traditional model-free policy updates. As such, it may be necessary to examine more complex settings, to reliably see a benefit from model-based search or planning, e.g., (Silver et al., 2016). Universality of RL benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that there is a striking lack of positive transfer between benchmarks. For example, despite the similarities in tasks and the same underlying MuJoCo simulator, the top performers in Gym and DMC fail to replicate their success on the opposing benchmark. Similarly, although DreamerV3 excels at Atari, these performance benefits do not translate to continuous control environments, underperforming TD3 in Gym and outright failing to learn the Dog and Humanoid tasks in DMC (see Appendix C). These findings show the limitations of single-benchmark evaluations, indicating that success on one benchmark may not translate easily to others, and highlights the need for more comprehensive benchmarks. Limitations. MR.Q is only the first step towards a new generation of general-purpose model-free deep RL algorithms. Many challenges remains for a fully general algorithm. In particular, MR.Q is not equipped to handle settings such as hard exploration tasks or non-Markovian environments. Another limitation is our evaluation only considers standard RL benchmarks. Although this allows direct comparison with other methods, established algorithms such as PPO have demonstrated their effectiveness in highly unique settings, such as team video games (Berner et al., 2019), drone racing (Kaufmann et al., 2023), and large language models (Achiam et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023). To demonstrate similar versatility, new algorithms must undergo the same rigorous testing across a range of tasks that is beyond the scope of any single study. As the community continues to push the boundaries of what is possible with deep RL, we believe that building simpler general-purpose algorithms has the potential to make this technology more accessible to a wider audience, ultimately enabling users to train agents with ease. Overview MR.Q is a general-purpose model-free RL algorithm that learns state-action embeddings via model-based objectives (reward prediction, dynamics prediction, terminal prediction), then uses those frozen embeddings as input to a standard TD3-style value function and policy. The key insight is that model-based representation learning implicitly produces features that are approximately linear with the true value function, enabling a single set of hyperparameters to work across diverse benchmarks. --- ## 2. Algorithm Architecture ### 2.1 Network Components Four distinct networks, trained in two decoupled stages: **Stage 1 — Encoder (trained end-to-end, updated every `T_target` steps)** | Network | Input | Output | Architecture | |---|---|---|---| | State Encoder `f_ω` | state `s` | `z_s` (dim 512) | CNN (images) or 3-layer MLP (vectors) | | State-Action Encoder `g_ω` | `(z_s, a)` | `z_sa` (dim 512) | 3-layer MLP | | Linear MDP Predictor `m` | `z_sa` | `(z_s', r, d)` | Single linear layer | **Stage 2 — RL (trained independently, updated every step)** | Network | Input | Output | Architecture | |---|---|---|---| | Value `Q_θ` (×2) | `z_sa` | scalar Q-value | 4-layer MLP | | Policy `π_φ` | `z_s` | action | 3-layer MLP | ### 2.2 State Encoder Details **For image observations (DMC-Visual, Atari):** ``` Conv2d(C_in, 32, kernel=3, stride=2) → ELU Conv2d(32, 32, kernel=3, stride=2) → ELU Conv2d(32, 32, kernel=3, stride=2) → ELU Conv2d(32, 32, kernel=3, stride=1) → ELU Flatten → Linear(1568, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU ``` - Input normalized: `state / 255.0 - 0.5` - Assumes 84×84 input → flattened size = 1568 **For vector observations (Gym, DMC-Proprioceptive):** ``` Linear(state_dim, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU Linear(512, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU Linear(512, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU ``` ### 2.3 State-Action Encoder Details ``` Linear(action_dim, 256) → ELU # action embedding z_a Concat([z_s, z_a]) # dim = 512 + 256 = 768 Linear(768, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU Linear(512, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU Linear(512, 512) # z_sa (no activation) Linear(512, output_dim) # linear MDP predictor m ``` - `output_dim` = `z_s_dim + reward_bins + 1` = `512 + 65 + 1 = 578` - The linear layer `m` maps `z_sa` to `(z_s', r_logits, d)` simultaneously ### 2.4 Value Network Details (×2 identical networks) ``` Linear(512, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU Linear(512, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU Linear(512, 512) → LayerNorm → ELU Linear(512, 1) ``` ### 2.5 Policy Network Details ``` Linear(512, 512) → LayerNorm → ReLU Linear(512, 512) → LayerNorm → ReLU Linear(512, action_dim) ``` - Continuous: `Tanh` final activation - Discrete: `Gumbel-Softmax(τ=10)` final activation ### 2.6 Weight Initialization - All linear layers: Xavier uniform initialization - All biases: 0 --- ## 3. Loss Functions ### 3.1 Encoder Loss The encoder is unrolled over a horizon `H_Enc = 5`. Given a subsequence `(s_0, a_0, r_1, d_1, s_1, ..., r_H, d_H, s_H)`: **Unrolling procedure:** ``` z̃^0 = f_ω(s_0) for t = 1 to H_Enc: z̃^t, r̃^t, d̃^t = g_ω(z̃^{t-1}, a^{t-1})^T · m z̄^t = f_{ω'}(s^t) # target encoder, stop gradient ``` **Total encoder loss:** ``` L_Encoder = Σ_{t=1}^{H_Enc} [ λ_Reward · L_Reward(r̃^t, r^t) + λ_Dynamics · L_Dynamics(z̃^t, z̄^t) + λ_Terminal · L_Terminal(d̃^t, d^t) ] ``` **Reward loss** — cross-entropy with two-hot encoding: ``` L_Reward(r̃, r) = CE(r̃, TwoHot(symexp(r))) ``` - 65 bins, range [-10, 10] in symlog space (effective range ≈ [-22k, 22k]) - `symexp(x) = sign(x) * (exp(|x|) - 1)` (Hafner et al. 2023) - Two-hot: distribute weight between the two nearest bins **Dynamics loss** — MSE between predicted and target state embedding: ``` L_Dynamics(z̃_s', z̄_s') = ||z̃_s' - z̄_s'||^2 ``` - Target `z̄_s'` comes from the **target encoder** `f_{ω'}` (stop gradient) **Terminal loss** — MSE: ``` L_Terminal(d̃, d) = (d̃ - d)^2 ``` - `λ_Terminal = 0` until the first terminal transition is observed in the replay buffer **Loss weights:** - `λ_Dynamics = 1.0` (implied as the base weight) - `λ_Reward = 0.1` - `λ_Terminal = 0.1` (after first terminal seen) ### 3.2 Value Loss Multi-step TD target with reward scaling: ``` ã_π = clip(π_{φ'}(s') + clip(ε, -c, c), -1, 1) # continuous ã_π = argmax(π_{φ'}(s') + clip(ε, -c, c)) # discrete ε ~ N(0, σ²), σ=0.2, c=0.3 Q̃'_j = r̄' · min_{j=1,2} Q_{θ'_j}(z_{s_{H_Q}, ã_π}) target = (1/r̄) · (Σ_{t=0}^{H_Q-1} γ^t r_t + γ^{H_Q} · Q̃'_j) L_Value(Q̃_i) = Huber(Q̃_i, target) ``` - `H_Q = 3` (multi-step return horizon) - `r̄` = mean absolute reward in replay buffer (updated at target sync) - `r̄'` = value of `r̄` at last target network copy - Huber loss used instead of MSE (for compatibility with LAP prioritized sampling) - Two value networks trained independently; minimum taken for target ### 3.3 Policy Loss Deterministic policy gradient with pre-activation regularization: ``` a_π = activ(z_π) # z_π is pre-activation output of policy network L_Policy(a_π) = -0.5 · Σ_{i∈{1,2}} Q̃_i(z_{s, a_π}) + λ_pre-activ · ||z_π||^2 ``` - `λ_pre-activ = 1e-5` - Continuous: `activ = Tanh` - Discrete: `activ = Gumbel-Softmax(τ=10)` - Gradients flow through `z_sa` but **not** back into the encoder (stop gradient on `z_s` when computing policy gradient) --- ## 4. Training Procedure ### 4.1 Update Schedule The key design choice is **synchronized periodic updates** every `T_target = 250` steps: ``` Every T_target steps: 1. Copy target networks: θ' ← θ, φ' ← φ, ω' ← ω 2. Update reward scaling: r̄' ← r̄, r̄ ← mean(|r| in replay buffer) For each of the T_target steps between syncs: 1. Collect one environment transition, add to replay buffer 2. Sample minibatch (LAP prioritized) 3. Update encoder (L_Encoder) 4. Update value networks (L_Value) — using frozen z_sa from encoder 5. Update policy (L_Policy) — using frozen z_s from encoder ``` **Critical implementation note:** The encoder is updated every step, but the target encoder `ω'` is only synced every `T_target` steps. The value and policy networks use embeddings computed from the **current** encoder `ω` but treat them as fixed inputs (stop gradient). ### 4.2 Replay Buffer and Sampling - **LAP (Loss-Adjusted Prioritized) sampling** (Fujimoto et al., 2020) - Priority = TD error (absolute difference between predicted and target Q-value) - Probability smoothing `α = 0.4` - Minimum priority = 1 (prevents zero-probability transitions) - Huber loss used in value update to correct for prioritization bias - Buffer capacity: 1M transitions - Minibatch size: 256 For the encoder loss, we need **sequential subsequences** of length `H_Enc + 1 = 6` from the replay buffer. Implementation Considerations and Ambiguities ### 11.1 Sequential Replay Buffer for Encoder Unrolling The encoder loss requires contiguous subsequences of length `H_Enc + 1 = 6`. The standard replay buffer stores individual transitions. Two approaches: - Store episode indices and sample contiguous windows (preferred) - Store fixed-length subsequences directly (wastes memory) - **Recommendation:** Implement a replay buffer that stores transitions with episode IDs and step indices, enabling contiguous sampling. ### 11.2 Gradient Flow - Encoder parameters `ω` receive gradients from `L_Encoder` only - Value network receives `z_sa` as input with **stop gradient** (detach from encoder) - Policy network receives `z_s` as input with **stop gradient** (detach from encoder) - During policy gradient, `z_sa` is recomputed from `z_s` (detached) and `a_π` — gradients flow through `g_ω` only for the action, not the state embedding ### 11.3 Reward Scaling Implementation - `r̄` = running mean of `|r|` across all transitions in the replay buffer - Updated at each target network sync: `r̄' ← r̄`, then recompute `r̄` - Used to normalize the value target (divide by `r̄`) and denormalize the target Q-value (multiply by `r̄'`) - Edge case: `r̄ = 0` (e.g., sparse reward early in training) — clamp to small positive value ### 11.4 Terminal Signal Handling - ## 2. `TwoHotEncoder` Class

This is the most complex component. It encodes scalar reward values into a soft categorical distribution over bins, enabling the cross-entropy reward loss described in Section 4.2.1 of the paper.

### 2.1 Purpose and Paper Alignment

The paper states: "Our reward loss function uses the cross entropy CE between the predicted reward r̃ and a two-hot encoding of the reward r." The bins are spaced at "increasing non-uniform intervals, according to symexp(x) = sign(x)(exp(|x|) − 1)."

From `config.yaml`:
- `reward_bins: 65`
- `reward_range_low: -10.0` (symlog space)
- `reward_range_high: 10.0` (symlog space)
- Effective range: symexp(±10) ≈ ±22026

### 2.2 `__init__(n_bins: int, low: float, high: float, device: torch.device)`

**Logic:**
- `n_bins = 65`, `low = -10.0`, `high = 10.0` (these are in symlog space, i.e., the bins are linearly spaced in symlog space, which means they are non-uniformly spaced in the original reward space)
- Create `self.bins` as a 1D float tensor of shape `(n_bins,)` using `torch.linspace(low, high, n_bins)` — this gives 65 values from -10 to 10 in symlog space
- Move `self.bins` to `device` and store as a buffer (not a parameter)
- Store `self.n_bins`, `self.device`
- The bins represent symlog-space values; actual reward values are mapped to symlog space before lookup

**Key insight:** The bins are in symlog space. When encoding a reward `r`, we first apply `symlog(r)` to get a value in approximately `[-10, 10]`, then find the two nearest bins in that space.

### 2.3 `symlog(x: Tensor) -> Tensor`

**Logic:**
- Formula: `sign(x) * log(|x| + 1)`
- This is a monotonic compression that maps large values to a smaller range
- For `x = 0`: result is 0
- For `x = 22026`: `symlog(22026) ≈ 10.0`
- Implementation: `torch.sign(x) * torch.log(torch.abs(x) + 1.0)`
- Must handle both scalar and batched tensors
- No clamping needed — the function is well-defined everywhere

### 2.4 `symexp(x: Tensor) -> Tensor`

**Logic:**
- Formula: `sign(x) * (exp(|x|) - 1)`
- This is the inverse of symlog
- For `x = 10.0`: `symexp(10.0) ≈ 22026`
- Implementation: `torch.sign(x) * (torch.exp(torch.abs(x)) - 1.0)`
- Must handle both scalar and batched tensors
- Note: for large `|x|`, this can produce very large values — this is expected behavior

### 2.5 `encode(x: Tensor) -> Tensor`

**Logic:**
- Input: `x` of shape `(batch,)` or `(batch, 1)` — scalar rewards per sample
- Output: float tensor of shape `(batch, n_bins)` — two-hot distribution

**Step-by-step:**

1. **Flatten input:** Ensure `x` has shape `(batch,)`

2. **Apply symlog:** `x_symlog = self.symlog(x)` — maps rewards to symlog space

3. **Clamp to bin range:** Clamp `x_symlog` to `[self.bins[0], self.bins[-1]]` to handle out-of-range values gracefully

4. **Find lower bin index:** Use `torch.searchsorted(self.bins, x_symlog)` to find the index where `x_symlog` would be inserted. This gives the index of the first bin greater than `x_symlog`. Subtract 1 to get the lower bin index. Clamp to `[0, n_bins - 2]` to avoid out-of-bounds.

5. **Compute interpolation weights:**
   - `lower_idx` = clamped index from step 4
   - `upper_idx` = `lower_idx + 1`
   - `lower_val = self.bins[lower_idx]`
   - `upper_val = self.bins[upper_idx]`
   - `upper_weight = (x_symlog - lower_val) / (upper_val - lower_val)` — fraction of the way from lower to upper bin
   - `lower_weight = 1.0 - upper_weight`
   - Both weights are in `[0, 1]` and sum to 1

6. **Construct two-hot tensor:**
   - Initialize `result = torch.zeros(batch, n_bins, device=self.device)`
   - Use `scatter_add` or direct indexing to place `lower_weight` at `lower_idx` and `upper_weight` at `upper_idx` for each batch element
   - Specifically: `result.scatter_(1, lower_idx.unsqueeze(1), lower_weight.unsqueeze(1))` and similarly for upper

7. **Return** `result` — each row sums to 1.0, has exactly two non-zero entries (or one if exactly on a bin boundary)

**Edge cases:**
- If `x_symlog` exactly equals a bin value, `upper_weight = 0` and `lower_weight = 1` — effectively a one-hot
- If `x_symlog` is below `bins[0]` or above `bins[-1]` after clamping, the weight goes entirely to the boundary bin

### 2.6 `decode(logits: Tensor) -> Tensor`

**Logic:**
- Input: `logits` of shape `(batch, n_bins)` — raw network output (before softmax)
- Output: scalar tensor of shape `(batch,)` — decoded reward values in original space

**Step-by-step:**

1. **Apply softmax:** `probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)` — converts logits to probability distribution over bins

2. **Compute expected bin value:** `expected_symlog = (probs * self.bins.unsqueeze(0)).sum(dim=-1)` — weighted average of bin positions in symlog space

3. **Apply symexp:** `result = self.symexp(expected_symlog)` — maps back to original reward space

4. **Return** `result` of shape `(batch,)`

**Note:** This is used for monitoring/debugging, not in the training loss. The training loss uses cross-entropy between predicted logits and the two-hot target directly.

## 6. `compute_aggregate_metrics(normalized_scores: List[float]) -> dict`

**Logic:**
- Computes mean, median, and IQM (Interquartile Mean) over a list of normalized scores
- These are the aggregate metrics reported in Tables 4-7 of the paper
- Input: flat list of normalized scores (one per environment, aggregated across the benchmark)

**Mean:**
- `mean = numpy.mean(normalized_scores)`

**Median:**
- `median = numpy.median(normalized_scores)`

**IQM (Interquartile Mean):**
- Sort scores, discard bottom 25% and top 25%, take mean of remaining 50%
- `sorted_scores = numpy.sort(normalized_scores)`
- `n = len(sorted_scores)`
- `lower = int(0.25 * n)`, `upper = int(0.75 * n)`
- `iqm = numpy.mean(sorted_scores[lower:upper])`

**Bootstrap CI for each metric:**
- Call `bootstrap_ci(data, n_bootstrap=10000, ci=0.95)` for each metric
- Return dict with keys: `'mean'`, `'median'`, `'iqm'`, `'mean_ci'`, `'median_ci'`, `'iqm_ci'`
- Each CI is a tuple `(lower, upper)`

## 7. `bootstrap_ci(data: ndarray, n_bootstrap: int, ci: float) -> Tuple[float, float]`

**Logic:**
- Computes a bootstrap confidence interval for the mean of `data`
- The paper reports 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals

**Stratified bootstrap procedure:**
- `n_bootstrap = 10000` (standard for reliable CI estimation)
- `ci = 0.95` → alpha = 0.025 for each tail
- For each bootstrap iteration:
  - Sample `len(data)` values from `data` with replacement
  - Compute the statistic (mean, median, or IQM — the caller decides which statistic to pass)
- Collect all bootstrap statistics
- Return the `(alpha/2)` and `(1 - alpha/2)` percentiles as the CI bounds

**Implementation note:** The function should accept a `statistic_fn` parameter (callable) so it can be reused for mean, median, and IQM. Alternatively, implement three separate functions. Given the design spec says it computes CI for the mean, we implement it generically with a default of `numpy.mean`.

**Practical implementation:**
```
bootstrap_stats = []
for _ in range(n_bootstrap):
    sample = numpy.random.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True)
    bootstrap_stats.append(statistic_fn(sample))
lower = numpy.percentile(bootstrap_stats, 100 * (1 - ci) / 2)
upper = numpy.percentile(bootstrap_stats, 100 * (1 + ci) / 2)
return (lower, upper)
```

## 8. `huber_loss(pred: Tensor, target: Tensor, delta: float = 1.0) -> Tensor`

**Logic:**
- Implements the Huber loss used in the value network update (Section 4.2.2)
- The paper uses Huber loss "instead of mean-squared error to eliminate bias from prioritized sampling" (LAP, Fujimoto et al. 2020)
- Formula:
  - If `|pred - target| <= delta`: `0.5 * (pred - target)^2`
  - If `|pred - target| > delta`: `delta * (|pred - target| - 0.5 * delta)`
- Returns element-wise loss tensor (same shape as input), **not** reduced — the caller handles reduction (mean or sum)
- This is equivalent to `torch.nn.functional.huber_loss(pred, target, reduction='none', delta=delta)`
- We implement it explicitly for clarity and to match the paper's description

**Why not use PyTorch's built-in?** PyTorch's `F.huber_loss` with `reduction='none'` is equivalent. We can wrap it for a clean interface, or implement from scratch. Either approach is valid — wrapping is simpler and less error-prone.

**Note on delta:** The paper does not specify delta explicitly. The standard value of 1.0 is used, consistent with TD3 and related work.

## 9. Key Design Decisions and Interactions

### 9.1 TwoHotEncoder and the Encoder Loss

In `agent.py`, the encoder loss calls:
```python
reward_target = two_hot.encode(batch_seq['rewards'][:, t])  # shape (batch, 65)
reward_loss = F.cross_entropy(r_logits, reward_target)       # CE with soft targets
```

The `encode` method must return a proper probability distribution (non-negative, sums to 1) for cross-entropy to work correctly. PyTorch's `F.cross_entropy` with soft targets requires the target to be a probability distribution when passed as a 2D tensor.

### 9.2 Device Consistency

`TwoHotEncoder` stores `self.bins` on the specified device. All operations in `encode` and `decode` must produce tensors on the same device as the input. The `self.bins` tensor must be moved to the correct device in `__init__`.

### 9.3 Numerical Stability in `encode`

The division `(x_symlog - lower_val) / (upper_val - lower_val)` can be numerically unstable if two adjacent bins are very close. Since bins are linearly spaced in symlog space with `n_bins=65` over `[-10, 10]`, the bin spacing is `20/64 ≈ 0.3125`, which is large enough to avoid numerical issues. No special handling needed.

### 9.4 Gradient Flow Through `encode`

The `encode` method is used to compute the **target** for the reward loss — it should not require gradients. The input rewards come from the replay buffer (numpy arrays converted to tensors), so they naturally have `requires_grad=False`. The `encode` method itself uses differentiable operations, but since it's applied to targets, gradients are not needed and `torch.no_grad()` context can be used by the caller.

### 9.5 Aggregate Metrics Computation

The `compute_aggregate_metrics` function is called in `main.py` after collecting final scores across all environments in a benchmark. The input is a list of normalized scores (one per environment), not per-seed scores. The bootstrap CI is computed over the cross-environment distribution, matching the paper's reporting methodology.
